analysis.one_liner: Limits handgun buyers to one handgun every 30 days and tightens dealer recordkeeping rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2008 with one cosponsor and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal crime for a person without a firearms dealer license to buy more than one handgun in any 30-day period, and for a dealer to sell a handgun to anyone the dealer knew or suspected had bought a handgun in the past 30 days. The point is to cut off the common trafficking method where a single buyer purchases a stack of handguns and resells them on the street. It would also raise the maximum prison term for dealers who falsify sales records from one year to five years, require gun stores to keep background-check records for at least 180 days instead of 24 hours, and repeal annual spending-bill riders that had blocked funding for the national background-check system.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in neighborhoods where trafficked handguns drive street violence, since bulk purchases that flood cities with cheap handguns would become a federal crime. Law-abiding buyers can still buy one handgun per month, and police, military, and law-enforcement purchases are exempted.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of neighborhoods hit by trafficked guns

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for an unlicensed buyer to purchase more than one handgun in any 30-day period, with the stated goal of reducing gun trafficking [S2][S3].

Prohibits a dealer from selling a handgun to anyone the dealer knows or has reasonable cause to believe bought another handgun within the past 30 days, placing responsibility on dealers who sell to suspected straw buyers [S2][S3].
Increases the maximum prison term for firearms dealers who make false statements in their sales records from one year to five years [S2][S3].
Requires background-check records to be retained for at least 180 days rather than being destroyed within 24 hours, preserving records that can later be used to trace crime guns [S2][S3].
Repeals appropriations riders that had blocked funding for the national instant criminal background check system and for systems that keep identifying records longer than 24 hours [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun dealers face a new prohibition on selling a second handgun to a buyer within 30 days and stronger recordkeeping duties, and unlicensed buyers who want multiple handguns in a month are barred. Firearm sellers lose the volume sales from bulk handgun purchases that fuel the resale market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun dealers and bulk handgun buyers

drawbacks.text: The one-handgun-per-30-days rule restricts purchases even by buyers with no connection to trafficking, including collectors and people who would otherwise buy two handguns for separate purposes; the bill's exceptions cover law enforcement, government purchases, one-for-one trades, and curios or relics, but not ordinary civilian buyers [S3].

Dealers carry new legal risk: they face liability for selling to a buyer they only have 'reasonable cause to believe' bought a handgun in the past 30 days, a standard that could be hard to apply at the counter [S3].
A single restriction on bulk handgun sales addresses one trafficking channel, not the full range of sources of crime guns, so its effect on violence depends on how large that channel is.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a narrow, well-documented trafficking practice: buying a stack of handguns at once for illegal resale. The cost to ordinary buyers is small (one handgun per month is a modest ceiling) and the record-retention change is mainly a bookkeeping burden on dealers, but the 'reasonable cause to believe' standard puts real discretion and legal exposure on dealers. It is a targeted measure rather than a comprehensive violence strategy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 26, 2008, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2009 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the End Gun Trafficking Act of 2008 on September 26, 2008, joined by Sen. Robert Menendez [S1][S3][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced; that was the last action in its history [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S1][S5].
It was introduced in the closing weeks of the 110th Congress, just before a national election, a period when few gun bills move.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm dealers and unlicensed bulk handgun buyers are better off, since the purchase limit never became law; anyone invested in leaving federal gun rules unchanged gained by the bill dying in committee without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun dealers and unchanged federal gun law

for.name: Sen. Frank R. Lautenberg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 26, 2008, and delivered introductory remarks [S5].

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction [S4][S3].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 26, 2008, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Long opposed one-handgun-per-month laws and has historically fought such purchase limits at the federal and state level.

sides.party_line_note: Both supporters were Democrats and there is no record of Republican support; the bill died in committee with only one cosponsor, so the record shows a one-party bill rather than a recorded party-line vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill bars dealers from selling a second handgun to the same unlicensed buyer within 30 days, raises penalties for falsified sales records to five years, and requires keeping background-check records for 180 days. It would end the bulk-sales business that can account for a large share of a dealer's volume, while ordinary one-per-month buyers are unaffected.

Manufacturers lose some legitimate bulk-order sales, but handgun demand overall is largely unchanged since buyers can still purchase one per month; the bill does not restrict manufacture or types of guns.

Traffickers who profit by buying multiple handguns at retail and reselling them on the street lose their main supply method; this resale channel is the channel through which street guns reach neighborhoods experiencing violence.
